So far so good this year, up at least 6% so far between the accounts (need to figure out the weighting still so my accounts are pretty out of whack now). Went decently large in the space theme to start and got some quick wins in $SATS (which is just a SpaceX proxy at this point) / $RDW and $MDALF (full ported my 401k into MDALF which isn't tracked yet. not a huge account but figured that was the place for such tomfoolery).

I did flip the $RDW for a quick ~35% but holding the other Space stuff. Planning to be a little more aggressive trading things this year, though I think this one still has legs. Space is going to be one of the 3 biggest themes of 2026 (up there with AI agents maybe humanoid robots though that feels more like 2027). Would happily rebuy this if we get a little pull back. Space is also fun to learn about. That said, everything repriced extremely fast already so we will have to see.

$GTLB not going great so far unfortunately so will probably continue doing a lot of work on this, especially around figuring out their exact customer base. Their relationships with Barclays, UBS etc seem pretty valuable. I am using Claude a tonne and extremely bullish on Anthropics prospects - I think $GTLB is poised to benefit from the relationship bigly, but we shall see.

Modest new position in $VSNT. The numbers here are absolutely ridiculous, P/FCF below 3. People see this as Comcasts fading cable assets, but to me there's a clear floor, if for no other reason than because CNBC (which they own) is highly valuable on any platform. For example, I pay for Sirius XM ONLY to listen to CNBC. If Spotify offered Versant more money to host it there, I would cancel $SIRI and get it there. This makes it highly valuable as a strategic asset. On top of this, Versant are increasingly pushing CNBC as a direct offering - probably I will just switch to that at some point. In a world where people pay $35 a month for WSJ or NYT, $15 a month for CNBC is nothing. I like Squawk Box w/ Becky Quick and crew, David Faber's stuff is always good, Squawk Box Asia is a solid listen while walking my dog around 5 pm PST... And though I worry about how large Cramer's audience is (and his key man status), I think the overall CNBC brand is strong. Prob my willingness to pay is actually quite high and they can just put me on an inflation+5% price increase schedule for the foreseeable future. Plan to keep ramping up my knowledge of this one.... could see it growing in size as i answer more questions.

JPM health conference will be a big market mover tomorrow. I don't expect it to have a huge impact on Novocure, but i did ape a little $RVMD for the buyout gamble. Will do pretty great for a 1 week hold if we get $140, and already up decent.

Slightly negative cash atm but plan to be back to around 90% net long by the end of the week and stay there most the year.

I think $7808 / cs lumber prob sells off when Japan opens, but like most earnings reports from this japaneseshitco, after crunching the numbers i will hold and maybe increase if we go low enough (with yen debt).

I wrote the name up here initially: https://t.co/UDzONOQ9eP

After a 30% decay in earnings this 'consolidated period' (first 2 quarters of FY2026) what makes me upbeat? or is it just cope?

1. continued stacking real estate. this is my whole view. if we stack real estate every quarter, i am a buyer.
2. year over year, rental revenue increased 20%. keep in mind, we're not reporting 'annualized rent', so when we buy new buildings each quarter, there is guaranteed growth in future quarters.
3. we are depreciating the real estate very fast! over 6m a year in cash flows are being sheltered by depreciation.
4. precut is where all the pain was due to lower housing starts, higher imported lumber costs, etc. awful margins! but we actually recovered a bit from last quarter and returned to profit here. so the reported consolidated numbers undersell the reality. that said, going forward the pre-cut business is not going to be the main business, which has been the narrative from the start.
5. real estate profits have not gone up despite our overall real estate portfolio increasing in size and rents up 20% YoY. i think profits will start going up again over time as rents increase in inflationary environment.
6. 92% of our profit this q was from rent - we are truely a REIT at this point, and a heavily discounted one at that.

In short, i think we are largely turning things around / inflecting. the core precut lumber business has returned from negative earnings last quarter. everything else is growing. we added more buildings. i still like it. it's a heavily discounted REIT with some bonus profitable businesses on top driving higher growth than one would expect.

of course, you will have to make up your own mind if you are in this one. no financial adviser is going to recommend this small japanese precut lumber company.

text:
Thoughts on Software
Was thinking "Ok I really need to figure exactly how much exposure I have to Software right now" over the weekend, but then realized "Oh I already built that, i just need to filter by industry in my ALPHAPORT portfolio (https://t.co/kOg9Vk77bA)".

As you can see in the link if you filter by industry - application software, its 23.24% of my net exposure after the sell offs, which is a little high for someone that believes that the hyperscalers largely take all the economics out of the software ecosystem.. but I think the distribution of outcomes for the three big positions is pretty good here. Could I be wrong? Sure, we will just have to see how it goes.

Of these 3, I personally think $GTLB is the most defensible though you are still paying a higher price. People are talking about the company like the sky is falling but GTLB has half of the Fortune 500 signed up, with no customer over 5% of revenue. These are easy throw away lines, but when you look at the actual deals with major financial institutions like UBS and Goldman Sachs, or Defense Contractors like $LMT or $NOC, these guys aren't just ripping out their giant CI/CD pipelines because the CEOs son built a shovelware video game with Claude Code on a Sunday. $1200 a year is also just not that much money for their Ultimate tier. I'm using $GTLB myself and while i'm an incredibly cheap human being, $1200 a year is below my line. I am spending 5x that on AI for sure right now. And when I ran a video game studio, we used to have artists that were earning 50-80k a year, and their Autodesk license for 3dsmax or Maya was costing us 3k a year! And they used other stuff too from $ADBE, like Substance Painter etc.

I also see $GTLB as the stodgier companies way into using more AI in their workflows.
"Ok we'll pay for Gitlab Ultimate and some Claude Code tokens, now tell us how to use AI better"
"Sure, you will be amazed at how much shit this can do now"
"Great".

A couple questions for the coming week are where I would close out the Tyler and Guidewire shorts (they both still seems expensive, but they legitimately have good businesses, they were just priced for perfection). Maybe 6x-7x rev.  You're still paying 13.5 billion for 1.27b of revenue with Guidewire. Mind boggling to me. You can come up with reasons that this might work out, but its hard for it to be absolutely amazing from this starting point. People will say "If you pay 13.5 billion for it now, and it grows 20% a year for 5 years, your ROI in 5 years is 20%".

Ok, but what about the year growth finally stalls. At some point it will. Maybe its in 7 years, maybe 10, but when growth goes from 20% to 10%, you will then lose 1/3 of your money. So its not as simple as just saying "10x rev is fine since they will pay 10x rev when I want to sell, since this is quality". Maybe you can perfectly time the exit the year before growth starts declining, but I certainly can't!

Companies I think are a little oversold and will still do well? $SAP, $CRM and $NOW are all unlikely to be ripped out because of some vibe coding. These services cross different verticals in the same business. A useful mental model is just to imagine telling all these teams that you are going to replace this software you all finally got working in between their various departments (in 2023 maybe?), with something George in the digital team builds over the weekend. Pretty lol if you ask me.

But for me, the starting prices are still quite high. $SAP looks particularly appealing of these 3, with what I view as a stickier product at a better price.

But you're still paying 235 billion euros for 36.5 billion of revenue. People will look at growth, or margin expansion, and make counter arguments, but to me, those things are much more fragile than sales if we have an uncertain future. Do I think people will rip out $SAP because of Claude Code? Very unlikely. Do i think that $SAP will be able to raise their prices at inflation + 4% for the foreseeable future because they have their customers completely locked in? I think that's more nebulous. Very possible, but not a certainty, and at 6.5x rev its still a little expensive for the risk. I think that one is getting quite close for me though, especially if I was rotating one of my losing software cos into it. I do also think that if there are software layoffs, for example $SAP themselves reduce headcount by 20%, the laid off engineers are going to need to get jobs somewhere - perhaps they will create competitor products because they have no choice. So we will see more software overall (more $GTLB seats),  but compressed margins. This is one reason it's important not to overpay for revenue - revenue is always defensible at scale. $SAP will ALWAYS work with a 5% net income margin. Maybe even a 10% net income margin. But at 10x sales, a 10% net income margin is a PE of 100. This is why, for me, 3x sales is really where I consider most companies as valid investments (30x PE at 10% net income margin, which is a pretty normal exit margin for most businesses. Still not that cheap!).

One thing this latest sell off has made really clear to me is how many investors legitimately think buying companies at 9-10x rev is cheap, or that using EV/FCF to value a software company is not a total fugazi. In a world of relative valuation and stock screeners, I think people have outsourced their critical thinking skills to a few metrics. "Here's where the company sits on the relative valuation PEG chart, LFG". How deeply have you thought about how margins actually inflect here? What leads to good business results for any given software business? Where are the risks? On the other hand, narratives that make no sense to me spread like wildfire. If you legitimately believe 50% of software engineers are going to be out of work, you should just buy way out $QQQ puts, because we are going to be talking about a much worse situation than $MNDY rerating to what I view as a much more reasonable valuation.

Anyway, https://t.co/prQtxvcJHO makes it really easy to track your portfolio like this by sector, long/short weights, etc (https://t.co/kOg9Vk77bA), and it's free if you use it with Interactive Brokers. Using Plaid, it also supports almost every other brokerage, although that is a paid feature ($10 a month though, a pittance!). If you want to sign up but have any trouble, feel free to DM me, i'll help you out.

Crazy it took this long for someone to reach out with a serious offer to Eric, his returns are nuts, especially given the amount of diversification and low net leverage (always below 80% and often way down in the 50s) he uses.
People will say you can't make money because the market is efficient so you should just buy index funds, but its people like Eric quickly taking the juice out of every inefficiencey that makes it efficient, doesn't mean its efficient for everyone. Can you do that too? Its possible. My mental model has always been the same as pro poker, where the vast majority of people lose, including a surprising amount of very smart people who just have the wrong temperament. The nice thing in investing though is you can throw darts at the board and still likely you will money, you have to be truly bad at investing to lose money long term since you have the wind in your sails.

2) When someone has this many positions, some trades won’t work out, and I strongly urge everyone to do their own research before taking a position in any stock/ETF they see, rather than blindly mimicking my trades.

3) My effective net exposure is a bit higher than what’s shown on the page, since shorts in ETFs such as $NVDQ and $DRIP are de facto longs (e.g. NVDQ goes down when $NVDA goes up, and vice versa).

4) Due to a professional opportunity that recently opened up, I might not be able to share this for very long. But until then, hopefully others can derive some value from it (and of course, constructive feedback on positions, industry/sector bets and portfolio construction is welcome).

Interesting development today from $KYIV. I still have a huge (~10%) $VEON position. VEON owns 83% of KYIV, as well as a bunch of other undervalued assets (that are worth its entire market cap on their own in my view).
$KYIV is putting up 25% USD rev/earnings growth with a PE of, i don't even know, like 5? 6? What are they going to do once the war in Ukraine ends?

I trimmed the tiniest amount today because i am trying to have a more diversified portfolio as i integrate more AI into my process (30 longs 50 shorts kind of thing) and wanted to buy some of the oversold stuff today. But sometimes I wonder if this should just be like, 20% of my portfolio or something. keep fluctuating between these two mentalities ha.

I wrote about KYIV and its relationship to VEON here: https://t.co/xC08eNKw0f

In the article I wrote that investing in VEON required not taking a position on the war, and that one should assume the worst. That said, since I wrote the article, Ukraine scored a large win, with plans to receive 90 billion in aid over the next 2 years. The big hold up right now is various companies in the Euro bickering over exactly who gets to send boatloads of weapons there. It seems pretty unlikely anything drastic is going to change from this point. That said, as I expressed in the Substack article, I don't think one should include calling the outcome of a war in one's investment thesis.
